question: None shared. This is the same pair as C-26: paper_b was repointed from the P-10 dedup stub to P-5 on 2026-08-29, and claim_b still names P-10. P-114 (Seifallahi et al., Kinect gait, pack pdf/P-115.txt) separates MCI from healthy controls; P-5 classifies AD/MCI/CN three ways from fundus photographs and OCT. The channels (gait/motor vs eye/retina) and the contrasts differ.
metric: Mismatch: binary accuracy (93%) vs the MCI-class precision (84.96%) of a three-class model.

figures.P-114: Binary MCI vs HC: accuracy 93% (n = 150; ANFIS protocol not stated), Wilson 0.878-0.961.
figures.P-5: Three-class accuracy 91.64%, AUC 96.78%; MCI-class precision 84.96% (image-level 5-fold CV; 29 MCI, 50 CN, 38 AD patients). No binary MCI-vs-CN accuracy.

reason: This duplicates C-26 and gets the same judgment. The channels differ (gait vs retinal imaging), the contrasts differ (binary vs three-class), and the figures are different statistics (accuracy vs MCI-class precision). The pair should be counted once.

quotes.quote: the proposed ANFIS classifier had values of 93%, 90%, and 91.5% for accuracy, sensitivity, and F-score, respectively when all extracted gait parameters in the DTW condition for the classification of elderly subjects to MCI and HC groups.
The proposed method achieved high precision rates of 84.96% and 80.90% in classifying MCI and positive test scores for cognitive impairment, respectively.
The neural network was applied to classify individuals with MCI, Alzheimer’s disease, and control participants with normal cognition.
